section.heading: 15.7. Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Coordinates
section.paragraph: In plane geometry the polar coordinate system is used to give a convenient description of certain curves and regions. (See Section 10.3.) Figure 1 enables us to recall the connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates. If the point $$P$$ has Cartesian coordinates $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and polar coordinates $$\left( {r,\theta} \right)$$ , then, from the figure,
$$\begin{array}{ll} {x = r\cos\theta} & { y = r\sin\theta} \\ {r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}} & { \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}} \end{array}$$

image.alt: Details Three line segments forming a right triangle are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The first line segment, labeled r, slopes upward to the right from the origin at an angle theta measured counterclockwise from the x axis until a point labeled P(r, theta) = P(x, y). From this point, labeled y, a vertical line segment descends downward to meet the x axis. The third line segment, labeled x, runs along the x axis from the origin to the point where the vertical line segment y meets the x axis. The three line segments form a right triangle with a horizontal base x, vertical side on the right y, and the hypotenuse r sloping downward to the left. The angle between x and y is a right angle.

section.paragraph: In three dimensions there is a coordinate system, called cylindrical coordinates, that is similar to polar coordinates and gives convenient descriptions of some commonly occurring surfaces and solids. As we will see, some triple integrals are much easier to evaluate in cylindrical coordinates.
section.heading: Cylindrical Coordinates
section.paragraph: In the cylindrical coordinate system, a point $$P$$ in three-dimensional space is represented by the ordered triple $$\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)$$ , where $$r$$ and $$\theta$$ are polar coordinates of the projection of $$P$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane and $$z$$ is the directed distance from the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane to $$P$$ . (See Figure 2.)

image.alt: Details Two line segments and two points are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first line segment, labeled r, lies in the first quadrant of the x y plane, begins at the origin, and slopes downward to the right at an angle theta from the x axis until a point labeled (r, theta, 0). The second line segment, labeled z, is vertical and runs parallel to the z axis from (r, theta, 0) to a point labeled P(r, theta, z).

figure.caption: The cylindrical coordinates of a point

example.heading: Example 1

list.item: (a) Plot the point with cylindrical coordinates $$\left( {2,2\pi/3,1} \right)$$ and find its rectangular coordinates.
(b) Find cylindrical coordinates of the point with rectangular coordinates $$\left( {3, - 3, - 7} \right)$$ .

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) The point with cylindrical coordinates $$\left( {2,2\pi/3,1} \right)$$ is plotted in Figure 3. From Equations 1, its rectangular coordinates are $$\begin{array}{l} {x = 2\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right) = - 1} \\ {y = 2\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\left( \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right) = \sqrt{3}} \\ {z = 1} \end{array}$$ Figure 3 Details Two line segments and a point are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first line segment lies in the second quadrant of the x y plane, begins at the origin, and slopes upward to the right at an angle 2 pi/3 from the x axis, and is labeled 2. The second line segment is vertical, begins from the point the first line segment ends, runs parallel to the z axis until a point labeled (2, 2 pi/3, 1), and is labeled 1. So the point is $$({- 1,\sqrt{3},1})$$ in rectangular coordinates.

(b) From Equations 2 and noting that $$\theta$$ is in quadrant IV of the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, we have $$\begin{array}{rll} r & = & {\sqrt{3^{2} + {({- 3})}^{2}} = 3\sqrt{2}} \\ {\tan\theta} & = & {{\frac{- 3}{3} = - 1} {so} {\theta = \frac{7\pi}{4} + 2n\pi}} \\ z & = & {- 7} \end{array}$$ Therefore one set of cylindrical coordinates is $$({3\sqrt{2},7\pi/4, - 7})$$ . Another is $$({3\sqrt{2}, - \pi/4, - 7})$$ . As with polar coordinates, there are infinitely many choices.

section.paragraph: Cylindrical coordinates are useful in problems that involve symmetry about an axis, and the $$z$$ -axis is chosen to coincide with this axis of symmetry. For instance, the axis of the circular cylinder with Cartesian equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = c^{ 2}$$ is the $$z$$ -axis. In cylindrical coordinates this cylinder has the very simple equation $$r = c$$ . (See Figure 4.) This is the reason for the name “cylindrical” coordinates. The graph of the equation $$\theta = c$$ is a vertical plane through the origin (see Figure 5), and the graph of the equation $$z = c$$ is a horizontal plane (see Figure 6).

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Describe the surface whose equation in cylindrical coordinates is $$z = r$$ .

Solution The equation says that the $$z$$ -value, or height, of each point on the surface is the same as $$r$$ , the distance from the point to the $$z$$ -axis. Because $$\theta$$ doesn’t appear, it can vary. So any horizontal trace in the plane $$z = k{\left( {k > 0} \right)}$$ is a circle of radius $$k$$ . These traces suggest that the surface is a cone. This prediction can be confirmed by converting the equation into rectangular coordinates. From the first equation in (2) we have
We recognize the equation $$z^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ (by comparison with Table 1 in Section 12.6) as being a circular cone whose axis is the $$z$$ -axis (see Figure 7).

The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The first cone has its tip at the origin and circular base parallel to the x y plane, with its center on the positive y axis. section.heading: Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Coordinates
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$E$$ is a type 1 region whose projection $$D$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is conveniently described in polar coordinates (see Figure 8). In particular, suppose that $$f$$ is continuous and
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {x,y,z} \right)|\left( {x,y} \right) \in D,u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right) \leqslant z \leqslant u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right)} \right\}$$
where $$D$$ is given in polar coordinates by
$$D = \left\{ {\left( {r,\theta} \right)|\alpha \leqslant \theta \leqslant \beta,h_{1}(\theta) \leqslant r \leqslant h_{2}(\theta)} \right\}$$

image.alt: Details A solid, a shaded region, and four line segments are graphed in the first octant of the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid, labeled E, resembles a sector of a thick ring with horizontal top and bottom sides. The base is a sector, labeled z = u_1(x, y), and the top side, labeled z = u_2(x, y), is also a sector. The projection of the solid is a shaded area labeled D, lying on the x y plane. D is a polar rectangle on the x y plane. The inner arc is labeled r = h_1(theta) and the outer arc is labeled r = h_2(theta). The left and right sides are labeled theta = alpha and theta = beta, respectively. Four vertical dashed line segments from the four corners of the base of E descend downward to meet the x y plane at the four corners of D.

section.paragraph: We know from Equation 15.6.6 that
$$\iiint\limits_{E}{f{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV} = {\iint\limits_{D}{\left\lbrack {\int_{u_{1}{({x,y})}}^{u_{2}{({x,y})}}{f\left( {x,y,z} \right)\mathit{dz}}} \right\rbrack\mathit{dA}}}}$$
But we also know how to evaluate double integrals in polar coordinates. In fact, combining Equation 3 with Equation 15.3.3, we obtain

$${\iiint\limits_{E}{f{({x,y,z})}\mathit{dV}}} = {\int_{\alpha}^{\beta}{\int_{h_{1}{(\theta)}}^{h_{2}{(\theta)}}{\int_{u_{1}{({r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta})}}^{u_{2}{({r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta})}}{f{({r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z})}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta}}}}$$

Formula 4 is the formula for triple integration in cylindrical coordinates. It says that we convert a triple integral from rectangular to cylindrical coordinates by writing $$x = r\cos\theta$$ , $$y = r\sin\theta$$ , leaving $$z$$ as it is, using the appropriate limits of integration for $$z$$ , $$r$$ , and $$\theta$$ , and replacing $$\mathit{dV}$$ by $$r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta$$ . (Figure 9 shows how to remember this.) It is worthwhile to use this formula when $$E$$ is a solid region easily described in cylindrical coordinates, and especially when the function $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ involves the expression $$x^{2} + y^{2}$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\iiint_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$E$$ is the solid that lies under the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ and above the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane (see Figure 10).

image.alt: Details The three dimensional rendering of a solid is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The solid is a paraboloid defined by z = 4 minus x^2 minus y^2, with its vertex on the positive z axis, opens downward until the x y plane. The circular base of the solid crosses the positive x and y axis at (2, 0, 0) and (0, 2, 0), respectively. Two vertical traces are drawn on the surface of the solid, both are parabolas opening downward sharing their vertices with the solid. The first trace has its arms falling on the first and third quadrant of the x y plane. The second trace has its arms falling on the second and fourth quadrant of the x y plane.

example.paragraph: Solution Because $$E$$ is symmetric about the $$z$$ -axis, we use cylindrical coordinates. In addition, cylindrical coordinates are appropriate because the paraboloid $$z = 4 - x^{2} - y^{2} = 4 - (x^{2} + y^{2})$$ is easily expressed in cylindrical coordinates as $$z = 4 - r^{2}$$ . The paraboloid intersects the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane in the circle $$r^{2} = 4$$ or, equivalently, $$r = 2$$ , so the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the disk $$r \leqslant 2$$ . Thus the region $$E$$ is given by
$$\left\{ {\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 2,0 \leqslant z \leqslant 4 - r^{2}} \right\}$$
and from Formula 4 we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2}\int_{0}^{4 - r^{2}}\left( r\cos\theta \right)^{2}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2}(r^{3}\cos^{2}\theta)\rbrack(4 - r^{2})\mathit{dr}d\theta} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos^{2}\theta d\theta\int_{0}^{2}(4r^{3} - r^{5})\mathit{dr}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack \theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta \right\rbrack_{0}^{2\pi}\left\lbrack r^{4} - \frac{1}{6}r^{6} \right\rbrack_{0}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{\iiint\limits_{E}x^{2}\mathit{dV}} = \frac{1}{2}(2\pi)(16 - \frac{32}{3}) = \frac{16}{3}\pi} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: A solid $$E$$ lies within the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ to the right of the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane, below the plane $$z = 4$$ , and above the paraboloid $$z = 1 - x^{2} - y^{2}$$ . (See Figure 12.) The density at any point is proportional to its distance from the axis of the cylinder. Find the mass of $$E$$ .

The top semicircular side is labeled z = 4 and has the center of its diameter at (0, 0, 4). A portion within the cylinder, which falls under the paraboloid labeled z = 1 - r^2, is shaded darker. $$E = \left\{ {\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant \pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 1,1 - r^{2} \leqslant z \leqslant 4} \right\}$$
Since the density at $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is proportional to the distance from the $$z$$ -axis, the density function is
where $$K$$ is the proportionality constant. Therefore, from Formula 15.6.13, the mass of $$E$$ is

$$\begin{array}{l} {m = {\iiint\limits_{E}{K\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\mathit{dV} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{1 - r^{2}}^{4}{{({Kr})}r\mathit{dz}\mathit{dr}d\theta}}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\int_{0}^{\pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{Kr^{2}{\lbrack{4 - {({1 - r^{2}})}}\rbrack}\mathit{dr}d\theta = K{\int_{0}^{\pi}{d\theta{\int_{0}^{1}{{({3r^{2} + r^{4}})}\mathit{dr}}}}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{m} = {\pi K\left\lbrack r^{3} + \frac{r^{5}}{5} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = \frac{6\pi K}{5}}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Solution This iterated integral is a triple integral over the solid region
$$E = {\{{\left( {x,y,z} \right)| - 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 2, - \sqrt{4 - x^{2}} \leqslant y \leqslant \sqrt{4 - x^{2}},\sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}} \leqslant z \leqslant 2}\}}$$

and the projection of $$E$$ onto the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the disk $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leqslant 4$$ . The lower surface of $$E$$ is the cone $$z = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ and its upper surface is the plane $$z = 2$$ . (See Figure 13.) This region has a much simpler description in cylindrical coordinates:
$$E = \left\{ {\left( {r,\theta,z} \right)|0 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 2\pi,0 \leqslant r \leqslant 2,r \leqslant z \leqslant 2} \right\}$$
